title: Source Code as a Transactional Abstraction
subtitle: Foundations for Transactional Source Control, with a Serverless Realization
author: Matthew Long
abstract: Source code and source control are now transactional abstractions: a repository is a database, a change is a transaction with a read set and a write set, landing is a commit under optimistic concurrency, a version is a snapshot, and derived data, Git included, are views of a transaction log. We argue that this is the next evolution in code, the move data lakes made from files to transactional tables, and assemble its foundations from a three-part series. The transaction model gives deterministic replay, immutable snapshots and serializability relative to declared read sets; its one anomaly, write skew between members of a landing batch, is removed by a pairwise check. Derived views are consistent at a snapshot when the key of each stored partition result determines that result, and a branch’s Git commit is a deterministic function of the log prefix. Composed, they let Git be built after landing without weakening the log’s guarantees; a reference realization on serverless primitives measures what that buys. On one controlled deploy, the two modes that built Git trees while landing landed 4 and 385 of 1,000 concurrent writers. Appending changesets in batches landed every writer in each of six bursts of 1,000, with landing p95 of 1.2 to 3.0 s and Git commits 3.2 to 5.4 s behind at p95. Commit p95 was under 1 s in two of those runs; no sustained landing rate has been measured and no workload has exercised the write-skew check.

title: A Transaction Log for Source Control
subtitle: Part I of Source Code as a Transactional Abstraction
author: Matthew Long
abstract: Source code and source control can now be treated as transactional abstractions: a repository is a database, a change is a transaction with a read set and a write set, landing is a commit under optimistic concurrency, and a version is a snapshot. This paper gives the transaction model on which that view rests. In Git, when many always-online agents write against one moving branch, every lost compare-and-swap race on the branch costs a rebase, a retest and a retry. In the model, commits are built on the server and recorded without moving any ref. A landing validates the change against every log entry written since its base and appends one hash-chained entry in the same atomic step as the ref update, performed by a serialized authority per repository. We prove replay determinism, snapshot immutability, refs that advance only along first-parent chains, and serializability, relative to declared read sets, of landings that need no line-level merge. The companion paper’s independence condition is exactly the condition under which two changes land without merging in either order. The model’s known gap is in group landing: a combiner that validates batch members only against the log admits write skew between them, and we give the check that removes it. In a reference implementation, the merge matched git merge-file on 300 of 300 random merges, and a changeset landing path landed 1,000 of 1,000 concurrent writers in each of six hosted bursts; a sustained landing rate remains unmeasured.

title: Partitioned Derived Data
subtitle: Part II of Source Code as a Transactional Abstraction
author: Matthew Long
abstract: Source code and source control can now be treated as transactional abstractions: a repository is a database, a change is a transaction with a read set and a write set, and a version is a snapshot. This paper supplies the part of that foundation that concerns derived data. We model search indexes, symbol tables, blame and work plans as views over the transaction log, maintained incrementally by partitioned jobs over immutable snapshots in the manner of Spark’s resilient distributed datasets, and stated over abstract primitives: an object store, a durable queue and stateless compute. We prove that a maintained view is consistent at a snapshot, equal to full recomputation, whenever the key under which each partition result is stored determines that result, a condition we call key sufficiency, and that the work per commit is then proportional to the size of the changed partitions. Content addressing subsumes recursion from parent commits and shares results across branches, while history-dependent views such as blame need the commit id as key. In the reference implementation, YonedaRepo on Cloudflare, the search key is a bare subtree id and is not sufficient, so a renamed or duplicated directory receives a view that names the wrong paths. An executed test confirms this view-consistency failure, and we give two repairs. A partitioned codemod is serializable under backward validation only if it declares its directory scope as a read. Indexing cost was not measured; the evidence is tests, including asserted rebuild counts of 3, 1 and 0.

title: A Cloud-Portable Architecture for Serverless Git
subtitle: Part III of Source Code as a Transactional Abstraction
author: Matthew Long
abstract: Source code and source control can now be treated as transactional abstractions: a repository is a database, a change is a transaction with read and write sets, and landing is a commit under optimistic concurrency. This Part measures what that transaction system costs on cloud primitives and where its serialized authority saturates. The architecture needs an object store, one serialized authority per repository, a durable queue, and stateless and container compute; the reference realization runs on Cloudflare. In six bursts of 1,000 writers on one repository, batched landing, which appends changesets to the log in one authority call per batch and builds Git objects afterwards, landed every change with landing p95 of 1.2 to 3.0 s and refused no commit, landing or read. Commit p95 was under 1 s in two of six runs, main’s Git commit lagged by 3.2 to 5.4 s at p95, and no sustained run exists. Landing modes that built Git trees on the landing path landed 4 and 385 of 1,000 on a controlled deploy. A closed queueing model over primitive service times reproduces earlier commit tails within 18 percent and bounds the measured landing rates. The evidence comes from one account, two clients and few runs per revision.
